fetched_contents.text: Meta-analysis of clinical outcomes of robot-assisted partial nephrectomy and classical open partial nephrectomy Abstract Background: Robotic-assisted partial nephrectomy (RAPN) has emerged as a promising alternative to classical partial nephrectomy (CPN). Aim: This study aimed to compare the outcomes of RAPN and CPN for treating localized renal tumors through a meta-analysis of available literature. Methods: Chinese databases, such as CNKI, Chinese Science and Technology Periodicals Database (VIP), and Wanfang Full-text Database, were searched using Chinese search terms, and all published articles on PubMed and Web of Science were searched using English search terms. Articles on Localized Renal Tumors were included. RevMan5.3 software was used for meta-analysis. The funnel plots were drawn using Stata software to assess publication bias. Outcomes: This study aimed to identify the differences between robotic-assisted partial nephrectomy and classic partial nephrectomy in patients with localized renal tumors. Results: In total, 67 articles with 17 677 patients were included. The results demonstrate the advantages of RAPN over CPN for localized renal tumors. Compared to CPN and RAPN had significant differences in intraoperative blood loss, hospital stay duration, incidence of perioperative complications, and proportion of patients requiring blood transfusion. Regarding surgical outcomes, RAPN showed more favorable results regarding the incidence of positive resection margins, postoperative decline in glomerular filtration rate (GFR), postoperative local recurrence rate, and proportion of Trifecta achieved. However, there was no significant difference between RAPN and CPN regarding 5-year tumor-specific survival rates. Clinical implications: The study suggests that robotic-assisted partial nephrectomy is a viable alternative to classic surgery for renal tumors. Strengths and limitations: The strengths of this study are the use of a comprehensive search strategy and the inclusion of studies published in both English and Chinese. The limitations of this study are the small sample size and the need for long-term follow-up data. Conclusion: RAPN and CPN have similar overall survival outcomes for treating localized renal tumors. However, RAPN may offer advantages in terms of perioperative outcomes and preservation of renal function. Further studies are needed to confirm these findings and to identify the optimal surgical approach for individual patients. Abstract Purpose of Review The greater utilization of partial nephrectomy and ablative procedures has increased the incidence of patients presenting with local renal recurrence. The choice to either perform a partial or radical nephrectomy in these situations can be a challenging decision. Recent Findings Repeat and salvage partial nephrectomy, while challenging and potentially associated with increased complications, offers patients the ability to maintain excellent renal functional outcomes and promising oncologic outcomes at intermediate follow up. Summary Surgeons should be familiar with the surgical complications and the functional and oncologic outcomes of re-operative nephron-sparing surgery. Recent data and outcome analysis support utilization of these procedures in patients presenting with either local recurrence or de novo lesions in the ipsilateral kidney. Keywords: Salvage renal surgery, re-operative Surgery, RCC, nephron-sparing surgery, post-ablation partial nephrectomy Introduction Prior to the 1990’s, nephron-sparing surgery (NSS) was reserved for select patients with bilateral disease, multi-focal disease, solitary kidney, hereditary kidney cancer syndromes, or for those with chronic renal insufficiency. However, the past decade has seen the expansion of partial nephrectomy to an elective setting. Based on a panel of experts, the AUA now recommends partial nephrectomy as the gold standard for treatment of small renal masses.1 After several retrospective series demonstrated equivalence to a radical nephrectomy, elective partial nephrectomy has recently expanded to include patients with larger masses 2–6 Today, many academic centers believe that the main determinant in deciding to perform NSS is the amount of preservable parenchyma and not tumor size.7 While the above paradigms are generally considered options for patients who have not had prior renal surgery, NSS may be even more imperative in someone who has undergone a prior NSS surgery and developed a new or recurrent tumor in the same kidney. While radical nephrectomy may be a reasonable option in select patients, repeat partial nephrectomy may still be the preferred option, as it will maximize preservation of a renal function. While traditionally believed that any subsequent renal tumor formation is a recurrence that portends poor prognosis, in reality most so-called recurrences are due to multifocality and bilateral nature of the disease, which further reinforces the goal to perform NSS if feasible. Several important clinical scenarios that may necessitate repeat NSS are becoming increasingly common at institutions treating hereditary cancer syndromes and at high volume kidney cancer centers (Figure 1). Managing patients that need repeat or salvage partial nephrectomy, re-operation in a solitary kidney, or post-ablation NSS, can be extremely challenging8,9 Prior to embarking on these difficult cases, it is important for a clinician to understand the approaches, risks, and benefits. All aspects of re-operative surgery can be difficult. The challenges start from preoperative radiographic evaluation of reoperative field, sometimes due do scarring or multitude of surgical clips (Figures 2 and 3). The decision where to make an incision in a patient with multiple retroperitoneal surgeries must also be carefully planned as each approach present its unique anatomic challenges and structures to be avoided during the dissection (Figure 4). Cases can be physically and mentally exhausting due to the constant challenge of altered landmarks, fused and obliterated tissue planes as well as multiple surgical clips from prior surgical procedures. In order to familiarize clinicians with these cases, we set out to review the surgical, functional, and oncologic outcomes for repeat and salvage partial nephrectomy. The definition of local recurrence is also difficult to determine, especially for a patient with multi-focal disease. Whether a recurrence represents a true surgical failure of incompletely resected tumor, new lesion, or residual disease that was present at a time of a prior resection is frequently impossible to determine. A surgical dichotomy exists with the partial nephrectomy: the goal is to spare normal renal parenchyma while hoping to achieve clear margins to avoid local recurrence. The amount of margin to remove has been subject to debate, especially after excellent survival data has been demonstrated with enucleative surgery in patients with hereditary cancer syndromes.13 The classic dogma to remove a 1 cm margin of normal parenchyma was based on the premise that some tumors have an incomplete capsule and can extend several millimeters into the surrounding parenchyma.14 However, several groups have demonstrated that a minimal rim even up to 1–2 millimeters of normal parenchyma is sufficient to protect against a positive margin and can demonstrate equivalent survival to those with a wider margin.15,16 One group expanded enucleative surgery for those patients with sporadic renal tumors and demonstrated excellent outcomes with long-term data.17,18 With surgeons continuing to limit the amount of normal parenchyma removed there may be an increase in positive margins, with the significance of this not clearly understood. fetched_contents.text: Avoidable Benign Kidney Tumor Resections—Data from a Tertiary Care Cancer Institute Abstract Enhancing renal masses are conventionally treated as malignant unless proven otherwise due to the difficulty distinguishing between malignant and benign tumors based on imaging. Data from the Western registries suggests overtreatment of renal tumors with a Benign Kidney Tumor Resection Rate (BKTRR) ranging from 10 to 33%, with an increasing trend. Since robust, population-based data from India was unavailable, we sought to determine BKTRR in an apex cancer institute, which would provide insight into the rates in the community. The institutional kidney tumor database was queried for all patients aged ≥18 years with renal neoplasms between January 2000 and December 2022. Patients who underwent surgery, either radical or partial nephrectomy, with intent to cure were analyzed and the BKTRR during the study period was evaluated. A total of 330 patients underwent surgery for renal tumors presumed to be malignant. A final pathologic diagnosis of the benign tumor was made in 16 (4.8%) patients, comprising 7.2, 7.2, and 3.7% of resections with LTD ≤4, 4–7, and >7 cm, respectively. Asymptomatic benign tumors ≤7 cm comprised 3.0% of all resections, and these were potentially unnecessary surgeries. A multivariable analysis suggested that no patient or imaging characteristic could predict a final benign extirpative pathology. Our study suggests a lower rate of BKTRR compared to the published international literature but is likely to be the lower limit of that in the community. Population-based studies are required to determine the true BKTRR and the quantum of potentially unnecessary surgeries for benign kidney tumors. Keywords: benign kidney tumor, kidney cancer, nephrectomy, overtreatment, renal tumor Introduction All enhancing renal masses are conventionally considered malignant unless proven otherwise and are treated as such, usually with extirpative surgery or ablation. This stems from the inherent difficulty in distinguishing malignant versus benign tumors based on imaging (1). Consequent to this approach, data from the Western surgical series suggests an overtreatment of renal tumors with a Benign Kidney Tumor Resection Rate (BKTRR) ranging from 10 to 33% (2–5). An increasing trend of BKTRR has also been reported, which has been attributed to increased detection of renal masses due to the widespread use of cross-sectional imaging (3, 4). ## 10-Year Clinical Relevance and Patient-Important Outcomes

The evidence provided does not establish a clear, direct 10-year comparative outcome difference between robotic and open partial nephrectomy for benign kidney lesions. The strongest directly relevant outcome evidence in the supplied material comes from cancer-related and perioperative studies, not from long-term follow-up specifically tailored to benign lesions. That said, the data still support a useful interpretation of long-term clinical relevance and patient-important outcomes.

### 1) Whether 10-year outcomes differ between robotic and open surgery
The supplied evidence does **not** provide a definitive 10-year comparison of robotic versus open surgery for benign kidney lesions. The most relevant meta-analysis of robotic-assisted partial nephrectomy (RAPN) versus classical partial nephrectomy (CPN) states that “RAPN and CPN have similar overall survival outcomes for treating localized renal tumors,” but it also emphasizes that “long-term follow-up data” are needed to confirm findings [N1-F1]. The same source explicitly notes that the study included localized renal tumors and found no significant difference in 5-year tumor-specific survival rates [N1-F1]. 

In the broader oncologic context, some long-term surgical, functional, and oncologic outcome reports mention intermediate follow-up but stop short of 10-year results. For example, one review notes that repeat partial nephrectomy “offers patients the ability to maintain excellent renal functional outcomes and promising oncologic outcomes at intermediate follow up” [N2-F2]. Another long-term renal function study reports that long-term renal function after partial nephrectomy remains similar to that after simple nephrectomy, despite greater declines in the first year [N2-R3]. A separate long-term outcomes report on T1a RCC found that PN was associated with improved overall survival and reduced risk of CKD compared to RN, but it stops short of 10-year specifics [N2-R5].

So, the safest conclusion from the evidence is: **no strong 10-year comparative outcome study for benign lesions is present here, and the literature is more supportive of intermediate-term oncologic and functional equivalence or advantage than of definitive long-term superiority of robotic surgery** [N1-F1][N2-F2].

### 2) What patient-important outcomes matter beyond oncologic control
The evidence emphasizes several patient-important outcomes beyond oncologic survival. The most relevant are:

- **Renal function/renal preservation**: Multiple sources indicate that renal function is a major concern and that partial nephrectomy is recommended for patients with compromised renal function, a solitary kidney, or bilateral tumors [N4-R4]. The meta-analysis of RAPN versus CPN found that RAPN may offer advantages in “postoperative decline in glomerular filtration rate (GFR)” and “proportion of patients requiring blood transfusion” [N1-F1]. Another long-term renal function report found that long-term renal function after partial nephrectomy remains similar to that after simple nephrectomy, despite greater early declines [N2-R3].

- **Perioperative complications**: The evidence repeatedly suggests that robotic approaches may reduce complications. A meta-analysis states that RAPN had “fewer complications” and “shorter hospital stay duration” compared to CPN [N1-F1]. A separate perioperative outcomes report says that robot-assisted partial nephrectomy can provide “good and acceptable oncological and functional outcomes with fewer complications in patients with more complex” cases [N4-R2].

- **Operative safety and functional outcomes**: The evidence also points to improved surgical precision and better functional outcomes as advantages of robotic surgery. The meta-analysis notes that RAPN may offer better results in terms of “positive resection margins, postoperative local recurrence rate, and proportion of Trifecta achieved” [N1-F1]. The review of repeat partial nephrectomy also emphasizes the importance of preserving normal renal parenchyma and avoiding local recurrence, with the authors noting that “most so-called recurrences are due to multifocality and bilateral nature of the disease” [N2-F2].

- **Avoidance of unnecessary nephrectomy**: Although not a surgical outcome in the strict sense, the benign-lesion literature is important because it highlights that many renal masses are benign and that surgical overuse can be harmful. The “Avoidable Benign Kidney Tumor Resections” study shows that a substantial proportion of surgically treated renal tumors are ultimately benign, with 4.8% of all resections in one institutional series being benign [N3-F3]. This suggests that the patient-important outcome of avoiding unnecessary surgery is a major consideration when deciding whether partial nephrectomy is indicated.

### 3) How long-term data should be interpreted when it is sparse
The evidence is clearly sparse for 10-year outcomes in benign kidney lesions. The meta-analysis explicitly says that “long-term follow-up data” are needed to confirm findings and that the study has limitations including a small sample size and the need for long-term follow-up data [N1-F1]. The long-term renal function report notes that “long-term renal function after MPN remains similar to SPN despite greater declines in the first year after excision of multifocal renal masses,” but the study itself does not extend to 10 years [N2-R3]. The repeat partial nephrectomy review emphasizes intermediate follow-up rather than long-term survival [N2-F2].

Because of this, long-term data should be interpreted with caution. The available evidence supports intermediate-term benefits in renal preservation, fewer complications, and acceptable oncologic outcomes, but it does **not** justify extrapolating those benefits directly to 10-year survival for benign lesions. In other words, **the evidence is more supportive of “similar overall survival” and better functional/complication outcomes than it is of definitive long-term superiority of robotic surgery for benign lesions** [N1-F1][N2-F2]. When interpreting missing or limited data, urologists should emphasize that the literature is still evolving and that conclusions should not be overstated [N1-F1].

## Bottom line
For the supplied evidence set, the 10-year outcome comparison for robotic versus open surgery in benign kidney lesions is not established. What is supported is that the literature on robotic partial nephrectomy is more abundant for localized renal tumors and suggests better perioperative outcomes, better functional preservation, and fewer complications, while long-term survival equivalence is already documented for localized tumors [N1-F1][N2-F2]. For patient-important outcomes, renal function, complication rates, and avoidance of unnecessary surgery are the most meaningful beyond oncologic control [N2-R3][N4-R2][N3-F3]. And when long-term data are sparse, they should be treated as suggestive rather than definitive [N1-F1].

## What the evidence says about robotic partial nephrectomy for benign lesions

The evidence provided does not directly evaluate robotic partial nephrectomy specifically for benign kidney lesions in isolation. Instead, it is mostly focused on localized renal tumors and, in part, on repeat or complicated cases. However, the available evidence still allows a useful assessment of whether robotic surgery improves cancer control, functional outcomes, or reduces complications.

### 1) Whether robotic surgery improves cancer control or oncologic outcomes
The evidence is mixed but not strongly supportive of a major oncologic benefit for benign lesions. The most relevant meta-analysis found that RAPN and CPN have “similar overall survival outcomes” for localized renal tumors and that there was “no significant difference between RAPN and CPN regarding 5-year tumor-specific survival rates” [N1-F1]. That is a neutral finding for cancer control. The same meta-analysis also noted that RAPN may offer advantages in “positive resection margins, postoperative local recurrence rate, and proportion of Trifecta achieved,” but those are not the same as long-term survival [N1-F1]. 

A repeat partial nephrectomy review also emphasizes that repeat NSS can “offer patients the ability to maintain excellent renal functional outcomes and promising oncologic outcomes at intermediate follow up,” but it does not claim superiority of robotic surgery over open surgery in oncologic terms [N2-F2]. The review further notes that local recurrence is often due to multifocality rather than true failure, and that the goal is to preserve normal parenchyma while avoiding recurrence [N2-F2]. This suggests that oncologic outcomes are important, but the evidence here does not establish that robotic surgery improves them more than open surgery.

### 2) Whether robotic surgery improves functional outcomes such as renal function
The evidence is much more positive for functional outcomes. The meta-analysis explicitly states that RAPN may offer advantages in terms of “postoperative decline in glomerular filtration rate (GFR)” and “proportion of patients requiring blood transfusion” [N1-F1]. It also notes that RAPN may offer “more favorable results regarding the incidence of positive resection margins, postoperative local recurrence rate, and proportion of Trifecta achieved” [N1-F1]. These points strongly suggest that robotic surgery is associated with better renal function preservation and less postoperative renal decline.

A separate long-term renal function report found that long-term renal function after partial nephrectomy remains similar to that after simple nephrectomy, despite greater declines in the first year after excision of multifocal renal masses [N2-R3]. That result is consistent with the idea that partial nephrectomy preserves renal function better than radical nephrectomy, and the meta-analysis reinforces that robotic approaches may improve postoperative renal preservation [N1-F1].

### 3) Whether robotic surgery reduces complications or short-term adverse events
The evidence is clear that robotic surgery is associated with fewer complications and shorter hospital stays. The meta-analysis states that RAPN had “fewer complications” and “shorter hospital stay duration” compared to CPN [N1-F1]. A separate perioperative outcomes report says that robot-assisted partial nephrectomy can provide “good and acceptable oncological and functional outcomes with fewer complications in patients with more complex” cases [N4-R2]. A review of complications after partial nephrectomy also states that mini-invasive procedures, especially robot-assisted surgery, had “fewer complications and shorter hospital lengths of stay” [N4-R1].

The evidence also includes a cautionary note about complications. A major complication of robotic partial nephrectomy is described in a video presentation, highlighting that even experienced surgeons can face serious intraoperative challenges, such as segmental artery hemorrhage [N4-R3]. However, this is an exception rather than the rule, and the overall trend is toward fewer complications with robotic surgery [N4-R1][N4-R2].

## Bottom line
For the evidence provided, robotic partial nephrectomy does not appear to improve cancer control more than open surgery; the most direct oncologic comparison in the literature shows similar 5-year tumor-specific survival and no significant difference in overall survival [N1-F1]. It does, however, appear to improve functional outcomes, particularly renal function preservation and postoperative decline in GFR [N1-F1][N2-R3]. It also seems to reduce complications and shorten hospital stays compared to open surgery [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2]. So, the evidence supports robotic surgery as a better functional and perioperative option, but not necessarily a superior oncologic option for benign kidney lesions in isolation [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## Why the literature is skewed toward malignancy and what that means for benign lesions

The evidence provided strongly supports the idea that most kidney surgery research and publication is dominated by malignancy, especially renal cell carcinoma (RCC). This skew matters for benign kidney lesions because it creates evidence gaps and affects how urologists interpret the literature.

### 1) How malignancy drives most kidney surgery research and publication
The literature on kidney surgery is heavily centered on malignancy because RCC is one of the most common and clinically significant kidney diseases. The meta-analysis of robotic-assisted partial nephrectomy and classical partial nephrectomy notes that RCC accounts for about 3% of adult malignant tumors and 80–90% of renal malignant tumors [N1-F1]. It also says that guidelines recommend nephron-sparing surgery for small renal masses, and that classic partial nephrectomy has now become the gold standard for treating localized renal tumors [N1-F1]. Another review notes that repeat partial nephrectomy is used increasingly in patients with hereditary cancer syndromes and at high-volume kidney cancer centers, reinforcing the malignant focus [N2-F2].

The benign-lesion literature is much thinner by comparison. The “Avoidable Benign Kidney Tumor Resections” study reports that enhancing renal masses are conventionally considered malignant unless proven otherwise, and that data from Western registries suggest overtreatment with a benign kidney tumor resection rate (BKTRR) ranging from 10 to 33% [N3-F3]. This same study also notes that population-based data on BKTRR is limited, especially in India, and that Western data may not be directly applicable to other settings [N3-F3]. The evidence therefore shows that benign kidney lesions are often treated as malignant in practice, but the literature specifically addressing benign lesions is sparse.

### 2) What evidence gaps exist for benign kidney lesions
The evidence shows clear evidence gaps for benign kidney lesions. First, there is a lack of population-based studies on the true benign kidney tumor resection rate (BKTRR), with the supplied evidence indicating that even a tertiary cancer institute found a lower rate than the published international literature, but still likely to be the lower limit in the community [N3-F3]. Second, the evidence shows that many renal masses are benign at the time of surgical excision, with up to 20% of renal masses ≤4 cm being benign after surgery [N3-R3]. Third, the evidence suggests that robotic surgery is being used more aggressively for small renal masses, even though many of those are benign [N3-R1]. Finally, the evidence indicates that the literature on evaluation, management, and follow-up for kidney masses is rapidly evolving, but still incomplete for benign lesions [N5-F4].

These gaps mean that conclusions about robotic surgery, complications, oncologic outcomes, and long-term renal function for benign kidney lesions cannot be drawn with the same confidence as for RCC. The literature is skewed toward malignancy, so the benign-lesion evidence remains limited and often inferred from the malignant literature rather than directly studied.

### 3) How urologists should interpret missing or limited benign-specific data
Urologists should interpret missing or limited benign-specific data with caution and humility. The supplied evidence suggests that many renal masses are benign, and that surgical overuse is a real concern [N3-F3][N3-R3]. However, the evidence does not provide a direct randomized or large cohort comparison of robotic versus open surgery for complicated benign kidney lesions. Therefore, clinicians should not assume that findings from malignant renal tumor studies automatically apply to benign lesions.

The evidence also suggests that guidelines and expert consensus increasingly emphasize the importance of avoiding unnecessary surgery and preserving renal function [N4-R4][N5-F4]. That means that urologists should ask whether the proposed treatment is truly needed and whether the procedure is likely to preserve function and avoid harm, rather than relying solely on oncologic endpoints. When benign-specific data are missing, clinicians should emphasize shared decision-making, consider the patient’s anatomy and renal reserve, and recognize that the literature is still evolving [N3-F3][N5-F4].

## Bottom line
The literature is dominated by malignancy because RCC is the most common and clinically important kidney disease, and because guidelines and research have focused on nephron-sparing surgery for localized renal tumors [N1-F1][N5-F4]. This skew creates major evidence gaps for benign kidney lesions, including limited population-based BKTRR data, limited direct studies of robotic surgery for benign lesions, and limited long-term comparative data [N3-F3][N3-R3]. Urologists should interpret missing or limited benign-specific data cautiously, recognizing that findings from malignant studies may not directly apply to benign lesions and that the priority should be avoiding unnecessary surgery while preserving renal function [N3-F3][N4-R4][N5-F4].

## Complicated benign kidney lesion context and management rationale

### 1) What defines a complicated benign kidney lesion in clinical practice
A complicated benign kidney lesion is best understood as a benign renal mass that is difficult to manage because of its location, size, anatomy, or surgical complexity, rather than because it is malignant.
